proposals.markdown:
## Morphology-Aware Query Expansion and Script Normalization for Serbian Support Search

**Company:** LinguaBot d.o.o. works in conversational AI. [C009] Challenge C009-CH1.  
**Researcher:** Stefan Dragić is a Full Professor in the Department of Mathematics and Informatics, Faculty of Sciences. [R0349]  
**Format:** joint project, one page.

### The problem
LinguaBot's Elasticsearch system returns no useful result for 18% of 12,000 real support queries sampled from one bank client. [C009-CH1] More than half of missed queries are caused by morphological mismatch or script confusion: Serbian inflects heavily (kartica, karticu, karticom) and users mix Cyrillic and Latin mid-sentence. [C009-CH1] The deployed stemmer is a Croatian stemmer paired with a simple script-normalisation step, and the system struggles with Serbian morphology and mixed-script input. [C009-CH1] Clients add new product terminology every quarter; the system must handle additions without full re-indexing, and the target is to keep the miss rate below 5%. [C009-CH1]

### Prior work
- A 2023 survey of stemming methods for inflected languages finds that linguistic knowledge-based techniques were widely used for highly inflected languages and reported higher accuracy than other techniques. [W4388666591]
- A 2020 study presents a sequence-to-sequence lemmatizer evaluated on 52 languages that reduces lemmatization errors by 19% on average over the prior best system. [W2911610808]

### Research questions
1. Does replacing the Croatian stemmer with a phoneme-based script-normalisation layer and Serbian morphological query expansion reduce the miss rate on LinguaBot's 85,000-pair dataset from 18% to below 5%, measured as the proportion of queries returning no useful result at rank 1–3?
2. Does an incremental indexing approach using streaming re-normalisation keep the miss rate below 5% after each quarterly terminology update, measured on a held-out set of 500 new-term queries per update cycle?
3. Does domain-adapted query expansion—trained on financial and telecom vocabulary from the annotated dataset—outperform a general Serbian morphological analyser on the same 85,000-pair benchmark, measured by mean reciprocal rank?

### Approach
- Replace the Croatian stemmer with a phoneme-based canonicalization layer drawn from the researcher's script-normalisation work, so that Cyrillic and Latin spellings of the same word map to a single index token regardless of mid-sentence script switches.
- Wrap the canonicalization layer with query expansion: at query time, generate transliteration variants and morphological forms (stemmed and lemmatized) using the researcher's transliteration-variant expansion method, then pass all variants to Elasticsearch as a disjunction query.
- Adapt the expansion tables to financial and telecom vocabulary by running the expansion pipeline over the company's 85,000-pair annotated dataset, with the company's two computational linguists validating domain-specific forms each iteration.
- Plug the updated pipeline into a streaming incremental indexing architecture so new terminology added each quarter triggers normalisation and expansion of only the new documents, with no full re-index required.

### Plan

| Period | Work | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Months 1–2 | Transfer the 85,000-pair dataset to the researcher's lab under a data agreement. A master's student installs the phoneme-based canonicalization module in LinguaBot's Elasticsearch test environment and runs the 12,000-query baseline evaluation. The company's linguists flag domain errors in the first output. | Baseline miss rate confirmed on the annotated dataset; a list of domain-specific normalisation errors from the linguists. |
| Months 3–4 | The master's student adapts the transliteration-variant query expansion tables to financial and telecom vocabulary using the annotated dataset. The researcher reviews the expansion logic; the linguists validate a 2,000-query sample. An A/B evaluation runs against the current production system. | Adapted expansion tables; A/B evaluation report showing miss rate against the <5% target. |
| Months 5–6 | Integrate the streaming incremental indexing module so quarterly terminology additions trigger partial re-normalisation only. Run a simulated quarterly update with 500 new-term queries. Deliver a technical handover document and a short conference paper draft. | Deployable pipeline passing the quarterly-update test; handover documentation; paper draft submitted. |

### First six months
- Week 1–2: The company and the researcher sign a data-sharing agreement; the company exports a de-identified version of the 85,000-pair dataset to the researcher's lab.
- Week 3–4: The master's student sets up a mirror Elasticsearch instance and replaces the Croatian stemmer with the phoneme-based canonicalization module; the researcher verifies the integration.
- Month 2: Run the full 12,000-query miss-rate evaluation on the mirror instance and compare against the 18% baseline; the company's two linguists review the first 500 misses for domain-specific errors.
- Month 2 end: Agree a prioritised list of financial and telecom term forms for the expansion tables, based on the linguists' error review, and set the go/no-go criterion for the month-4 A/B test.

### What each side brings
- **Company:** Annotated dataset of around 85,000 query-response pairs across all clients. [C009-CH1, C009] Measured baseline of 18% miss rate on 12,000 real support queries, giving a concrete starting point and a clear <5% target. [C009-CH1] Two computational linguists on staff focused exclusively on Serbian morphology and dialect variation. [C009, C009-CH1] Existing Elasticsearch deployment with a basic Croatian stemmer already in production, and spaCy with custom Serbian morphological components in the technology stack. [C009-CH1, C009]
- **Faculty:** Stefan Dragić co-authored work on phoneme-based canonicalization for mixed Cyrillic-Latin Serbian text retrieval. [SYN-PUB-04279, SYN-PUB-04278] Stefan Dragić co-authored work on query expansion through transliteration variants for Serbian mixed-script search. [SYN-PUB-04280] Stefan Dragić co-authored work on a real-time streaming indexing architecture for incremental document processing with script normalization at scale. [SYN-PUB-02734] Stefan Dragić is open to joint projects with companies managing large Serbian-language document collections and has collaborated with a legaltech startup on customizing search modules for Serbian text under an 18-month contract research agreement. [R0349]

### Why this pair
LinguaBot has a precisely measured problem—18% miss rate, a clear domain (financial and telecom support), a large annotated benchmark, and two linguists who can validate outputs—but lacks the script-normalisation and morphological expansion methods needed to go below 5%. Stefan Dragić brings exactly those methods (phoneme-based canonicalization, transliteration-variant query expansion, streaming incremental indexing for Serbian), developed and published for mixed-script Serbian retrieval, plus prior experience delivering a custom search module for an industry partner. Neither could do it alone: the company brings the domain data, the live Elasticsearch environment, and the linguistic validators; Stefan Dragić brings the normalisation and expansion methods; the day-to-day implementation work could be carried out by a master's student or junior researcher from the faculty group, subject to agreement at project start.

- Stefan Dragić is open to joint projects with companies managing large Serbian-language document collections and has prior experience delivering custom search modules to an industry partner. [R0349]

### Risks and constraints
- The publications cover general Serbian document collections; coverage of financial and telecom support terminology as found in C009-CH1 is not evidenced in the record. [C009-CH1, SYN-PUB-04279, SYN-PUB-04278]
- C009-CH1 states the budget for tooling or data work is around 8,000 EUR and that a testable solution is expected within six months. [C009-CH1]

### Agreed up front (proposed)
- Publication: results may be submitted for publication after a 30-day review by LinguaBot; the company may request removal of client-identifying terminology before submission.

- Data access: LinguaBot provides the 85,000-pair dataset in de-identified form to the researcher's lab for the duration of the project; the dataset is deleted from lab systems within 30 days of project close.
- Preconditions: the data-sharing agreement is signed and the Elasticsearch mirror environment is accessible to the master's student before month-1 work begins; the approximately 8,000 EUR budget is allocated to tooling or data work; the two sides should confirm at project start exactly how it is split across compute, data preparation, and any staff costs.

## Agent-Based Scanning Pipeline to Cut Penetration-Test Reconnaissance from Four Days to One

**Company:** Sentinel Byte preduzetnik works in cybersecurity. [C012] Challenge C012-CH1.  
**Researcher:** Árpád Nagy is a Full Professor in the Department of Computing and Control Engineering, Faculty of Technical Sciences. [R0564]  
**Format:** joint project, one page.

### The problem
Each penetration-test engagement takes about two weeks, with a few days spent on reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration; clients are requesting continuous testing and retesting after patches, which the company cannot sustain at current billing rates without automation. [C012-CH1] Existing Bash scripts break when tool versions change — Nessus has changed its output format twice since the scripts were written — and the diff step for detecting changes between scans requires manual review to manage noise from edge cases. [C012/blog/2024-04-02/Why we wrote our own reconnaissance scripts and why we are about to stop] Multiple real clients — including two municipalities and a regional medical supply company — are asking for continuous or frequent retesting, but the company cannot offer retest work without adding staff unless the initial phase is cut from four days to one. [C012-CH1]

### Research questions
1. Can an agent-based pipeline complete host discovery, service enumeration, and vulnerability data collection on a target network and deliver a structured JSON report within one working day, measured against the company's current four-day baseline on three anonymised past engagement scopes?
2. Does an incremental change-detection step between successive scans reduce manual review time compared with the company's current diff approach, measured by the number of false-positive change alerts on a controlled test network with known-good and known-changed states?

### Approach
- Apply the agent-based scanning architecture from the researcher's host-discovery and topology-mapping work to orchestrate Nmap and Nessus scans against target network scopes, replacing the fragile Bash wrapper with a versioned, tool-agnostic coordination layer.
- Use the ontology-driven normalisation and SPARQL integration method from the vulnerability data normalisation work to ingest Nessus and Nmap output into a unified internal representation that is insulated from tool version changes.
- Implement the incremental graph-update method from the researcher's attack graph work to detect and classify changes between scans — new hosts, closed ports, new or patched CVEs — with a noise threshold tuned on the company's test environment.
- Apply the LLM-assisted structured extraction method to convert the unified internal representation into the JSON report schema the company's manual testers receive, including suggested remediation priorities.

### Plan

| Period | Work | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Months 1–3 | Set up the test environment in the researcher's network-emulation laboratory. Collect and anonymise three past engagement scopes as baseline data. Build the agent-based scanning coordination layer and the ontology-driven normalisation module. Baseline timing figures for all three scopes. |

Run end-to-end timing trials on the three anonymised scopes and one live retest engagement. Measure false-positive change alerts against known-good and known-changed test states. | A complete prototype meeting the one-day target (or a documented gap with a remediation plan). A change-detection accuracy report. A structured JSON report sample reviewed by the company's testers. A short technical note suitable for submission. |

### First six months

- Month 2: A student intern from the researcher's laboratory builds the agent-based coordination layer and the ontology-driven normalisation module; Nikola Kovačević dedicates roughly two days per week to the project, primarily on tooling and automation topics.

- Months 4–6: The student implements and calibrates the incremental change-detection module and LLM report generator; the company engineer validates each module on a live retest engagement; the pair reviews results and prepares the technical note.

### What each side brings
- **Company:** Nikola Kovačević can dedicate roughly two days per week to a collaborative development project, primarily on tooling and automation topics. [C012] Existing Nmap and Nessus toolchain and Git-versioned test documentation. [C012] A budget of roughly 3,000 to 5,000 euros covering the prototype development collaboration. [C012-CH1]

[SYN-PUB-06546] Árpád Nagy co-authored work on LLM-assisted parsing of raw scanner output into a fixed JSON schema covering host identity, open services, CVEs, and remediation priorities. [SYN-PUB-06551]

### Why this pair
Sentinel Byte has a concrete, measurable bottleneck — four days of fragile, manual-adjacent work — and real clients ready to consume a faster service, but lacks the methods to build a reliable, version-stable pipeline with principled change detection. Árpád Nagy brings published, tested methods for exactly the four sub-problems that make up that bottleneck: agent-based orchestration, normalisation across tool versions, incremental change detection, and structured report generation. Neither could reach the target alone: the company brings the engagement data, the live toolchain, and the practitioner judgement needed to validate the prototype against real pentesting work; the researcher brings the laboratory infrastructure, student internship capacity, and the published methods that address the fragile-script problems.

proposals.markdown:
## System-Level AFE and Radio Duty-Cycle Optimisation to Cut KL-Patch 72 Active Current by 35%

**Company:** Kardiolink a.d. works in medtech and digital health. [C005] Challenge C005-CH1.  
**Researcher:** Filip Mijatović is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications, Faculty of Technical Sciences. [R0905]  
**Format:** joint project, one page.

### The problem
The KL-Patch 72 consumes 18 mAh per day when BLE is active, against a 54 mAh lithium cell, leaving insufficient margin for the full 72-hour wear period on active patients. [C005-CH1] Kardiolink must reduce active current draw by at least 35% while keeping the ECG sampling rate at 250 Hz or above to preserve clinical signal validity. [C005-CH1] The team has tuned BLE advertising intervals, adopted BLE 5.0 long-range PHY, and switched to a lower-power MCU variant, and is now within a few milliamps of what firmware changes alone can achieve; the device runs FreeRTOS on a Nordic nRF52840. [C005-CH1, C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems] Kardiolink currently deploys approximately 2,200 KL-Patch 72 devices per month and plans to grow to 6,000 active patches per month over the following two years. [C005-CH2, C005]

### Prior work
- A 2019 study derives power-consumption models for duty-cycling schemes and determines the maximum energy budget an additional wake-up radio can consume before duty-cycling becomes more efficient in IoT networks. [W2942345566]
- A 2022 study shows that combining dynamic voltage and frequency scaling with duty-cycling on an MSP430-based sensor node significantly reduces normalised power while sustaining throughput in high-data IoT applications. [W4311857643]

### Research questions
1. Can event-driven radio wake-up techniques — adapted from 868 MHz body-area network designs to the nRF52840's BLE radio — reduce the radio's share of active current by at least 35%, measured by before-and-after current profiles on the Keysight N6705C across a continuous 72-hour recording session at 250 Hz?
2. Can board-level analogue front-end redesign, guided by sub-1 µA biopotential amplifier principles, reduce the AFE's quiescent current contribution sufficiently to meet the residual current budget after radio optimisation, measured against the current profile of the unmodified patch at 250 Hz sampling?

### Approach

**Company:** DriveLogic Vojvodina d.o.o. works in automotive and mobility software. [C018] Challenge C018-CH1.  
**Researcher:** Mirjana Vidaković is a Full Professor in the Department of Computing and Control Engineering, Faculty of Technical Sciences. [R0948]  
**Format:** joint project, one page.

### The problem
DriveLogic manually generates approximately 3,200 AUTOSAR software component configuration files per project, occupying two senior engineers for three weeks. [C018-CH1] The bottleneck makes the company uncompetitive on price-sensitive bids. [C018-CH1] The mapping logic between the customer-provided System Extract and the final ARXML configuration set must be automated, and the output must be a reviewable first-draft configuration set that engineers check and correct. [C018-CH1]

### Research questions
1. Can a transformation chain reading a System Extract and writing DaVinci API calls generate a complete, rule-conformant ARXML SWC configuration draft within one working day? Measured as end-to-end wall-clock time on the two most recent project baselines, with conformance checked against the company's existing hand-authored ARXML sets.
2. How many manual corrections do engineers need to make to the generated first-draft, compared with starting from scratch? Measured as the count of post-generation edits logged during review of the generated set against the hand-authored baseline on the same two projects.

### Approach
- Parse the customer-provided System Extract into an intermediate model using the AUTOSAR metamodel concepts from the researcher's SWC-descriptor work, capturing port interfaces, runnables, and component topology needed to drive DaVinci API calls.
- Apply model-transformation rules—drawing on ATL and QVT-O patterns from the researcher's comparative transformation work—to map System Extract elements to ARXML SWC configuration constructs, with explicit guard predicates that route exception cases to a review log rather than failing silently.
- Generate ARXML files and DaVinci API invocations using Acceleo or Xpand templates, following the template-based generation patterns from the researcher's RTE-stub and Adaptive-Platform work, with ARXML-aware diffing applied after generation so engineers see only the delta against any prior baseline.
- Validate the generated set incrementally: change-impact analysis drawn from the researcher's incremental-generation work limits regeneration to components affected by a System Extract update, keeping subsequent runs well under one working day even as projects evolve.

## Unsupervised Site-Adaptive Anomaly Detection for Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP On-Device Deployment

**Company:** ArmaturaSec d.o.o. works in cybersecurity. [C001] Challenge C001-CH1.  
**Researcher:** Krisztina Kiss is a Full Professor in the Department of Computing and Control Engineering, Faculty of Technical Sciences. [R1008]  
**Format:** joint project, one page.

### The problem
ArmaturaSec has terabytes of normal Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP traffic from three years of client deployments but zero confirmed attack examples, making supervised classifiers unusable. [C001-CH1] Training on public ICS datasets produced unacceptable false positive rates in real deployments because the models cannot capture site-specific polling patterns and register usage. [C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection] The detector must run on-device on the company's existing hardware without degrading packet forwarding latency, and must be explainable to plant managers in plain language. [C001-CH1, C001]

### Prior work
- DeepAnT uses unlabelled time-series data and a CNN-based predictor to forecast the next timestamp, then an anomaly detector module tags each timestamp as normal or abnormal; it detects point anomalies, contextual anomalies, and discords. [W2906498146]

### Research questions
1. Can a per-site one-class classifier trained only on the company's own Modbus TCP traffic archives detect behaviour that deviates from that site's normal polling patterns, measured by precision and recall on a held-out set of synthetic deviations injected into real captures?
2. Does beta-mixture-model threshold calibration from unlabelled operational data reduce the false positive rate at BACnet/IP sites to an agreed acceptable level, measured against the company engineer's manual review of flagged events over a 30-day live trial?
3. Can a quantisation-and-pruning compressed model meet on-device inference latency requirements on the company's target hardware, measured by packet forwarding delay before and after model deployment?

### Approach
- Extract per-session and per-register-address feature vectors from Modbus TCP captures using the statistical baseline modelling approach from the researcher's one-class classification work on Modbus/TCP, then train a per-site one-class classifier on the company's own traffic archives — not public datasets.
- Apply beta mixture model threshold calibration to each site's unlabelled operational stream, estimating the contamination fraction without requiring labelled attack examples, so the decision boundary adapts to each deployment's traffic volume and periodicity.
- Compress the trained per-site models using quantisation and pruning to fit within the memory and compute budget of the company's on-device hardware, verifying that packet forwarding latency does not increase beyond an agreed ceiling.
- Map model output scores to a small set of named alert categories tied to observable protocol events (e.g. unexpected function code, new device address, register write outside normal range), giving plant managers plain-language flags without requiring them to interpret detector scores.

### Plan

| Period | Work | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Months 1–3 | Company engineer transfers a representative subset of Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP captures (covering at least three distinct client sites) to the researcher's lab under the data-sharing agreement. Researcher's master's student parses captures using the company's existing C/Rust protocol parser, extracts session-level and register-level feature vectors, and documents the feature set. Company engineer validates feature semantics against known site configurations. | Labelled feature dataset covering three sites; agreed feature specification document. |
| Months 4–6 | Master's student trains per-site one-class classifiers (one-class SVM and statistical baseline models) on Modbus TCP features. Beta mixture model calibration is applied to set detection thresholds without labelled attacks. Synthetic deviations are injected into held-out captures to produce an evaluation set. Models are evaluated on precision, recall, and false positive rate. | Baseline detector for Modbus TCP with calibrated thresholds; internal evaluation report; draft of first joint paper. |
| Months 7–9 | Extend the approach to BACnet/IP features. Apply quantisation and pruning to compress both Modbus and BACnet models to fit the company's on-device hardware. Company engineer integrates compressed models into the firmware codebase and measures packet forwarding latency. Alert categories are defined jointly and mapped to plain-language descriptions for the plant-manager interface. | Compressed models integrated into firmware; latency benchmark showing on-device feasibility; plain-language alert taxonomy. |
| Months 10–12 | Run a 30-day live trial at one consenting client site. Company engineer monitors alerts; false positives reviewed manually. Threshold recalibration applied if needed. Findings written up; final paper submitted. Go/no-go decision on further deployment. | Live-trial report; submitted joint paper; recommendation for next deployment phase. |

### First six months
- Month 1 — data transfer: company engineer identifies three representative client site captures (with client consent confirmed), anonymises as needed, and transfers to the researcher's lab under a signed data-sharing agreement.
- Month 1–2 — feature extraction setup: master's student integrates the company's existing C/Rust Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP parser as a library, runs it against transferred captures, and produces session-level and register-level feature vectors; company engineer reviews output for correctness.
- Month 2–3 — baseline characterisation: master's student plots traffic periodicity, function-code distributions, and register-address ranges per site to document what normal looks like at each; researcher and company engineer agree on which features are site-adaptive versus protocol-generic.

### What each side brings
- **Company:** Several terabytes of Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP network traffic captures from consenting clients, collected over three years.
